steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper arguing that biases in crowdsourced NLU benchmarks can come from the annotation instructions themselves (what we call instruction bias). Cover the background on crowdsourced benchmarks, our hypothesis, what our study of recent benchmarks finds, the effect on models, and the takeaways.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Benchmarks drive NLU progress; created by crowdsourcing with instructions
- Known crowdsourcing biases, usually blamed on annotators
- Our hypothesis: bias starts in the task instructions (instruction bias)
- Study of 14 benchmarks: patterns in instructions propagate to data
- Why this matters: tasks broader than the patterns
- Effect on model performance
- Conclusion and recommendations

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - benchmarks pivotal for NLU progress in recent years (cite)
  - now mostly crowdsourced; crowdworkers write examples following instructions from dataset creators (cite)
  - instructions = short task description + several examples (cite)
- Known biases
  - crowdsourced data shows biases -> overestimated model performance (cite)
  - usually attributed to annotators: writing style, background knowledge (cite); related work in § A
- Hypothesis
  - bias originates early: in designing the annotation task
  - instructions guide annotators -> crowdworkers follow specific patterns -> propagated and over-represented in data
  - example: Quoref dataset (cite): ~36% of instruction examples start "What is the name", ~59% of collected instances
- Study
  - "instruction bias", 14 recent NLU benchmarks
  - evident in most; ~73% of instruction examples on average share a few clear patterns
  - patterns propagated by annotators; cover ~61% of instances on average
  - instruction examples play critical role in data collection and example distribution
- Why it matters
  - hard to represent a task with a few examples; bias makes it harder; task and reasoning broader than patterns
  - co-reference resolution, temporal commonsense reasoning, numerical reasoning vs. Quoref ("what is the name…"), MC-Taco ("how long…"), DROP ("how many field goals…")
- Effect on models
  - performance overestimated; models often fail to generalize beyond instruction patterns
  - higher pattern frequency in training set -> often larger gap between pattern and non-pattern examples
  - large models generally less sensitive
- Conclusion
  - instruction bias widespread; overestimation
  - concrete recommendations for monitoring and alleviating it in future data collection
  - implications for learning-by-instructions paradigm (cite): crowdsourcing instructions used in model training

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years benchmarks have been very important for making progress in Natural Language Understanding (NLU). Today most NLU benchmarks are created by crowdsourcing, where crowdworkers write examples by following annotation instructions that the dataset creators wrote. These instructions usually have a short description of the task and several examples.

This method has been very successful, but past studies showed that crowdsourced data often has different biases, and these biases make model performance look better than it is. People usually attribute these biases to the annotators, for example to their writing style and background knowledge (more related work is discussed in § A).

In this work we propose that the biases in crowdsourced NLU benchmarks often start at an early point of data collection, namely when the annotation task is designed. Specifically, our hypothesis is that the task instructions written by dataset creators, which are the guiding principles annotators use to do the task, often make crowdworkers follow certain patterns, and these patterns then get propagated into the dataset and are over-represented in the collected data. For example, \sim 36\% of the instruction examples for the Quoref dataset start with “What is the name”, and the same pattern is found in \sim 59\% of the collected instances.

We test this hypothesis with a broad study of this kind of bias, which we call instruction bias, in 14 recent NLU benchmarks. We find that most of these datasets have instruction bias, with \sim 73\% of the instruction examples on average sharing a few clear patterns. We also find that annotators propagate these patterns into the collected data, where they cover \sim 61\% of the instances on average. This means instruction examples play a critical role in data collection and in the distribution of the resulting examples.

- Why it matters
  - hard to represent a task with a few examples; bias makes it harder; task and reasoning broader than patterns
  - co-reference resolution, temporal commonsense reasoning, numerical reasoning vs. Quoref ("what is the name…"), MC-Taco ("how long…"), DROP ("how many field goals…")
- Effect on models
  - performance overestimated; models often fail to generalize beyond instruction patterns
  - higher pattern frequency in training set -> often larger gap between pattern and non-pattern examples
  - large models generally less sensitive
- Conclusion
  - instruction bias widespread; overestimation
  - concrete recommendations for monitoring and alleviating it in future data collection
  - implications for learning-by-instructions paradigm (cite): crowdsourcing instructions used in model training

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years benchmarks have been very important for making progress in Natural Language Understanding (NLU). Today most NLU benchmarks are created by crowdsourcing, where crowdworkers write examples by following annotation instructions that the dataset creators wrote. These instructions usually have a short description of the task and several examples.

This method has been very successful, but past studies showed that crowdsourced data often has different biases, and these biases make model performance look better than it is. People usually attribute these biases to the annotators, for example to their writing style and background knowledge (more related work is discussed in § A).

In this work we propose that the biases in crowdsourced NLU benchmarks often start at an early point of data collection, namely when the annotation task is designed. Specifically, our hypothesis is that the task instructions written by dataset creators, which are the guiding principles annotators use to do the task, often make crowdworkers follow certain patterns, and these patterns then get propagated into the dataset and are over-represented in the collected data. For example, \sim 36\% of the instruction examples for the Quoref dataset start with “What is the name”, and the same pattern is found in \sim 59\% of the collected instances.

We test this hypothesis with a broad study of this kind of bias, which we call instruction bias, in 14 recent NLU benchmarks. We find that most of these datasets have instruction bias, with \sim 73\% of the instruction examples on average sharing a few clear patterns. We also find that annotators propagate these patterns into the collected data, where they cover \sim 61\% of the instances on average. This means instruction examples play a critical role in data collection and in the distribution of the resulting examples.

It is hard to represent a task with only a few examples, and bias in the instruction examples makes it even harder, because a task and the reasoning it needs are broader than the instruction patterns. For example, co-reference resolution, temporal commonsense reasoning and numerical reasoning are much broader tasks than the common patterns in the Quoref (“what is the name…”), MC-Taco (“how long…”) and DROP (“how many field goals…”) datasets.

We look at how instruction bias affects model performance, and we show that it makes performance look higher than it is and that models often do not generalize beyond the instruction patterns. We also see that when instruction patterns are more frequent in the training set, the performance gap between pattern and non-pattern examples often gets bigger, and that large models are generally less sensitive to instruction bias.

To conclude, our work shows that instruction bias exists widely in NLU benchmarks and often leads to overestimated model performance. From the study we derive concrete recommendations for monitoring and reducing this bias in future data collection. More broadly, the findings also have implications for the recent learning-by-instructions paradigm, where crowdsourcing instructions are used to train models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Benchmarks have proven pivotal for driving progress in Natural Language Understanding (NLU) in recent years [1,2,3]. Nowadays, NLU benchmarks are mostly created through crowdsourcing, where crowdworkers write examples following annotation instructions written by dataset creators [4,5,6]. The instructions typically include a short description of the task, along with several examples [7,8,9].

Despite the success of this method, past studies have shown that data collected through crowdsourcing often exhibits various biases that lead to overestimation of model performance [10,11,12,13,14,15,16,17]. Such biases are often attributed to annotator-related biases, such as writing style and background knowledge [11,18] (see more discussion on related work in § A).

In this work, we propose that biases in crowdsourced NLU benchmarks often originate at an early stage of the data collection process: the design of the annotation task. In particular, we hypothesize that the task instructions provided by dataset creators, which serve as the guiding principles for annotators, often lead crowdworkers to follow specific patterns, which are then propagated to the dataset and over-represented in the collected data. For instance, \sim 36\% of the instruction examples for the Quoref dataset [7] start with “What is the name”, and this same pattern appears in \sim 59\% of the collected instances.

To test our hypothesis, we conduct a broad study of this form of bias, which we term instruction bias, in 14 recent NLU benchmarks. We find that instruction bias is evident in most of these datasets: \sim 73\% of instruction examples on average share a few clear patterns. Moreover, these patterns are propagated by annotators to the collected data, where they cover \sim 61\% of the instances on average. This suggests that instruction examples play a critical role in the data collection process and in the resulting example distribution.

Representing a task with a few examples is difficult, and bias in instruction examples makes it even more difficult, since a task and its associated reasoning have a larger scope than the instruction patterns. For example, co-reference resolution, temporal commonsense reasoning, and numerical reasoning are much broader tasks than the prevalent patterns in the Quoref (“what is the name…”), MC-Taco (“how long…”) and DROP (“how many field goals…”) datasets.

We investigate the effect of instruction bias on model performance and show that performance is overestimated due to instruction bias and that models often fail to generalize beyond instruction patterns. Moreover, we observe that a higher frequency of instruction patterns in the training set often increases the performance gap between pattern and non-pattern examples, and that large models are generally less sensitive to instruction bias.

In conclusion, our work shows that instruction bias is widespread in NLU benchmarks and often leads to an overestimation of model performance. Based on our study, we derive concrete recommendations for monitoring and alleviating this bias in future data collection efforts. More broadly, our findings also have implications for the recent learning-by-instructions paradigm [19,20], in which crowdsourcing instructions are used in model training.
